newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - Feb 25.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - Feb 25.

text.p: The following stories were reported in Tuesday's electronic version of The Wall Street Journal:
* Applied Magnetics launched a hostile bid for Read-Rite valued at $36 a share, or $1.7 billion, and said it would begin a proxy fight to oust the Read-Rite board.

* News Corp said it would buy 50 percent of EchoStar Communications DISH.O in a deal valued at about $1 billion, creating a new direct-broadcast satellite venture that would challenge cable television providers.
* Ultramar Diamond Shamrock is in talks to acquire Total Petroleum in a deal valued at more than $400 million plus about $430 in debt assumption.
* The Supreme Court said it will review a lower-court's decision to limit the membership of federally chartered credit unions.
* AT&T's plan to use wireless technology to link home telephones to its network could speed its entry into the local phone market, but such an effort would be costly.
* About 65 million viewers watched "Schindler's List" on General Electric's NBC television network, which could jolt advertising and programming on network TV.
* Chubb Corp agreed to sell its life insurance business to Jefferson-Pilot for about $875 million.
* Two executives at smokeless tobacco company UST resigned amid questions about the company's performance.
* American Electric Power and Public Service Co of Colorado agreed to acquire Britain's Yorkshire Electricity for about $2.4 billion.
* The Dow industrials rose 76.58 to 7,008.20. Bond prices drifted and the dollar fell.
* Petroleum and natural-gas prices continued to fall amid unseasonably mild temperatures.
* Motorola is losing sales to rivals in the U.S. digital telephone business, according to an industry research report.
* Japan's Yoshitomi Pharmaceuticals agreed to acquire Green Cross, which has been mired in a scandal involving HIV-tainted blood products.
* Don't count your sheep before they're cloned.

That was much of Wall Street's reaction yesterday to the news that a Scottish scientist successfully cloned an adult sheep in Edinburgh. Though there was a flurry of buying yesterday - a lot of it from small investors - in shares of companies involved in finding commercial uses for genetics research, most investors cautioned that it's far from certain that the cloning will beget profits in stocks. -- Heard on the Street.

* Bonds gave up ground in slow trading as traders, lacking new economic figures of any significance and awaiting an important address by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan later this week, focused on continued weakness in the dollar. -- Credit Markets.
